strengths: PST addresses a meaningful gap in evaluating language-conditioned image generation: gender associations can change when two social roles appear together. Testing both occupation pairings and organizational hierarchy is relevant to multimodal NLP and fairness research.

The occupational evaluation systematically crosses 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations and reverses their positions. Three human annotators per image, with reported Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92, provide credible support for the perceived-gender labels.

The reported distributions support increased stereotype adherence under paired prompting, particularly for male-stereotyped occupations. Explicit prompt templates, occupation inventories, and detailed results help readers examine this finding. FairCritic’s substantial aggregate score reductions provide encouraging preliminary mitigation evidence.
weaknesses: The main fairness interpretation exceeds what the metric establishes. SS averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposing imbalances to cancel. In Table 1, the single-person occupational scores of 50 and −30 average to 10 despite substantial gender imbalance in both groups. Likewise, FairCritic’s near-zero aggregate scores, including the separate stereotype-group averages, can conceal disparities across individual occupations. These results establish reduced average stereotype adherence, not 'near-perfect fairness' under the paper’s stated criterion of equal gender probabilities for each role. Conditional gender distributions and a non-cancelling disparity measure are needed.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproduction. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but does not adequately document the operational critic prompts, number and grouping of inspected images, feedback insertion procedure, or separation between feedback-generating samples and evaluation samples. These are essential methodological details; a promised code release does not resolve their absence.

The comparison with prompt intervention does not establish FairCritic’s claimed superiority. Table 2 evaluates occupational intervention on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic across the full occupational set. Identical evaluation sets and generation budgets are needed. Fixed-feedback and resampling controls would also help establish whether image-conditioned criticism contributes beyond additional instructions or another generation attempt.

Sampling uncertainty limits the finer conclusions. Only three single-person images are sampled per identity, occupational PST has one run, and confidence intervals are absent. This particularly weakens occupation-level amplification rankings and claims of reliably near-zero mitigation outcomes. Additionally, the headline percentage with any stereotyped subject needs a reference distribution: independent gender-balanced draws already produce at least one stereotype-adhering subject in 75% of two-person images. The reported 'both' statistic provides stronger evidence than that headline.

Annotation agreement does not establish that generated subjects fulfill the requested occupations, power relationships, and positions. No systematic adherence evaluation is reported before or after mitigation, so reduced scores could partly reflect changes in task fulfillment. The treatment of 'Cannot Identify' responses, annotation disagreements, and missing or extra subjects is also unclear.

The supported scope is an English, binary perceived-gender audit of DALL·E 3; broader claims about T2I systems and more complex generation settings remain untested. Reporting also needs reconciliation, notably the repeated totals of 944 versus 1,952 constructed prompts. The central measurement, comparative-evaluation, and reproducibility gaps prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present, but appear addressable through revisions and focused experiments for the next cycle.
